newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Fiji angers Beijing with Taiwan pact.
newsitem.headline: Fiji angers Beijing with Taiwan pact.

text.p: The Pacific island Fiji on Friday signed a mutual-recognition pact with Taiwan, earning a warning from ally China not to fall for ploys by Taiwan to break free of its Beijing-imposed diplomatic isolation.
"The status (of the mutual-recognition pact) is just below establishment of diplomatic relations," Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang told reporters after a signing ceremoney.
"(The pact) recognises us as an official government and a sovereign nation. We feel this is very important," Chang said.
Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government has diplomatic ties with only 30 states, mainly in Africa and central America. Most of the world recognises Beijing's communist government.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and refuses to recognise any country having official relations with the island.
China parried the Taiwan-Fiji pact by admonishing friendly states to guard against ploys by Taiwan to win recognition and warning of damage to their ties with Beijing.
"Taiwan province is an inalienable part of China," a Chinese Foreign Ministry official said in Beijing when asked about Fiji's friendly gesture toward Taiwan.
"...we are firmly opposed to countries that have diplomatic relations with China (also) having official relations or carrying out official contacts with Taiwan," he said.
All countries should recognise China in line with United Nations resolutions, he added.
"We urge these countries to be on guard against the political plots by the Taiwan authorities so as to prevent any damage to the relations between the two countries," he said.
He did not say whether China would break with Fiji.
Chinese parliament chief Qiao Shi was quoted on September 9 in the party flagship People's Daily as hailing Fiji's "one China" stance and wanting more cooperation with Pacific states.
Chang signed the communique with Fijian Foreign Minister Filipe Bole in the second day of Bole's five-day Taipei visit.
Chang said Taiwan would push for full diplomatic relations with the former British possession in the South Pacific.
Foreign ministry officials said Fiji was the third state to enter into this kind of "mutual recognition" pact with the Republic of China government.
Pacific neighbours Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea, both of which also recognise China, signed similar agreements with Taiwan in September 1992 and May 1996, respectively, they said.
A foreign ministry statement said Bole would discuss setting up a trade office in Taipei during his stay.
Taiwan has provided agricultural assistance to Fiji since 1978 and opened a trade office there in 1987.
Beijing won the latest round in its battle with Taipei for diplomatic allies, wooing back Niger in August four years after the African state switched ties to Taiwan.
